# Yellow fever

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Zoonoses and vector-borne diseases > Yellow fever*

[Original Article Link](/library/U50bjg)

---

## Summary

Yellow <u>fever</u> is an acute viral infection caused by the <u>yellow fever virus</u>. Primates are the main reservoir of the <u>virus</u>, which is usually transmitted through bites from infected mosquitoes. Yellow <u>fever</u> is <u>endemic</u> in large parts of South America and Africa. The <u>incubation period</u> is 3–6 days, and the majority of affected individuals remain asymptomatic or experience only mild symptoms. Symptomatic patients initially present with nonspecific symptoms such as sudden-onset <u>fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>, <u>headaches</u>, chills, <u>nausea</u>, and <u>myalgia</u>. Approx. 15% of these patients progress to the most serious stage of the disease, which can present with life-threatening <u>hemorrhagic fever</u> and organ failure. There is no causal treatment available, making prevention of crucial importance. A single dose of live-attenuated <u>vaccine</u> provides lifelong protection for most individuals.

---

## Epidemiology

* Yellow <u>fever</u> is <u>endemic</u> in tropical regions of South America and Sub-Saharan Africa.

* Asia, Europe, North America, and Australia are free of yellow <u>fever</u> (except for occasional imported cases).





> [!NOTE]
> Yellow <u>fever</u> is <u>endemic</u> in large parts of South America and Africa.

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>yellow fever virus</u>

* Genus: <u>flavivirus</u>, type of <u>arbovirus</u>

* Genetics: single-stranded, <u>positive-sense</u>, linear <u>RNA virus</u>

* Appearance: enveloped, icosahedral

* Transmission

* <u>Vectors</u>: mosquitoes;  (primarily <u>Aedes aegypti</u>  )

* Main reservoir: primates (human and non-human)

* Different transmission cycles (depending on local circumstances and geography)





![Mosquito (Aedes aegypti)](media/d8ypnmnq8x8r88cfsbx3kc48.jpg)

Mosquito (Aedes aegypti)




References:[[2]](/library/I9aYK5)[[3]](/library/r9afK5)

## Clinical features

* Incubation time: 3–6 days

* Clinical features

* The majority of infected individuals remain asymptomatic.

* In symptomatic patients: classic progression in three stages
1. * Period of infection (3–4 days) 

* Sudden onset of high <u>fever</u> (up to 41.0Â°C (106Â°F))

* <u>Headaches</u>, chills

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>
2. * Period of remission (up to 2 days)
* Easing of symptoms and decline in <u>fever</u>
3. * Period of intoxication (only in ∼ 15% of symptomatic patients)

* Hemorrhage (<u>epistaxis</u>, <u>mucosal</u> bleeding, <u>melena</u>, <u>hematuria</u>, black <u>vomiting</u>)

* <u>Multiorgan dysfunction</u> (e.g., acute <u>kidney</u> and <u>liver</u> failure)

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>, severe <u>jaundice</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Most patients remain asymptomatic or experience only mild symptoms.




References:[[4]](/library/kfammP)[[5]](/library/79a4K5)

---

## Diagnosis

* Laboratory tests

* ↑ <u>Transaminases</u>

* <u>Leukopenia</u>

* In period of intoxication

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u>, ↑ <u>PTT</u>

* Signs of organ failure (see <u>acute liver failure</u>, <u>acute renal failure</u>)

* <u>Virus</u> detection

* <u>PCR</u>

* <u>ELISA</u>

* <u>Liver biopsy</u>

* Used for definitive diagnosis (e.g., postmortem)

* Must not be done while the patient has an active yellow <u>fever</u> infection

* May show <u>Councilman bodies</u> (eosinophilic <u>apoptotic</u> globules)





> [!NOTE]
> The best test to rule out yellow <u>fever</u> infection is <u>PCR</u>, particularly in the absence of overt symptoms such as <u>fever</u>, <u>headaches</u>, and chills.




References:[[2]](/library/I9aYK5)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Influenza</u>

* Viral <u>hepatitis</u> (e.g., <u>hepatitis A</u>)

* Other <u>viral hemorrhagic fevers</u> (e.g., <u>Dengue hemorrhagic fever</u>)

* <u>Malaria</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

* Symptomatic treatment

* No specific antiviral treatment is available





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>NSAIDs</u> that increase the risk of bleeding (e.g., <u>aspirin</u>, <u>ibuprofen</u>, <u>naproxen</u>) in patients with confirmed or suspected yellow <u>fever</u> infection!




References:[[5]](/library/79a4K5)

---

## Prevention

### <u>Vaccination</u> [[2]](/library/I9aYK5)[[6]](/library/H9aKK5)[[7]](/library/Ef18LT0)




* The yellow fever vaccine is a <u>live-attenuated vaccine</u> administered subcutaneously.

* Indications: individuals 9 months to 60 years of age ≥ 10 days prior to [[7]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* International travel to areas with <u>endemic</u> yellow <u>fever</u> (see “<u>Immunizations before travel</u>”)

* Handling of yellow <u>fever</u> strains (e.g., in laboratory or research jobs)

* A single lifetime dose is typically sufficient; some individuals may require a booster.  [[7]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* Contraindications include: [[8]](/library/mgWVDk0)

* History of <u>anaphylaxis</u> to any <u>vaccine</u> component (e.g., eggs, latex in a prefilled syringe)

* Age < 9 months [[7]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* <u>Absolute contraindication</u> if < 6 months of age (risk of <u>encephalitis</u>)

* <u>Relative contraindication</u> if 6–8 months of age

* <u>Contraindications for live vaccines</u>





> [!TIP]
> When contraindications are present, consider the individual's specific risks and benefits and use shared-decision making to decide whether to immunize.




> [!TIP]
> If state supplies of <u>yellow fever vaccine</u> are limited, direct international travelers to the following <u>CDC</u> website (wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/search-for-stamaril-clinics) for US providers of imported, non-<u>FDA</u> approved <u>yellow fever vaccines</u>. [[7]](/library/Ef18LT0)
